Kazakhstan’s Kurultai Election is a Domestic Test for Central Asia’s Regional Ambitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
19:13:00 UTC
04:13:00 KST

On August 23, Kazakhstan will elect the first members of its new Kurultai, a 145-seat unicameral legislature established under the constitution that entered into force in July. Seven political parties are contesting the election in a single nationwide constituency. All seats will be filled through proportional representation, with no directly appointed deputies. A consequential question is what the newly elected institution will be expected to do.
The distribution of seats and the composition of the new legislature will naturally dominate domestic attention. But the election also has implications beyond Kazakhstan. It will test whether the country can support its increasingly active regional and international diplomacy with an institution capable of translating agreements into legislation, allocating resources over several years, and overseeing their implementation.
This matters because Central Asia’s position in international politics is changing. The region is no longer viewed solely as a space in which larger powers compete for influence. Central Asian states are developing their own positions on connectivity, trade, energy, water management, critical minerals and digital development. They are also engaging collectively with China, the European Union, the United States, the Gulf states and other partners through a growing number of regional formats.
Kazakhstan has been particularly active in this process. Its pragmatic and multivector foreign policy, economic weight and geographic position have enabled it to act as both a regional convenor and a bridge between major markets. Yet geopolitical agency cannot be sustained through presidential diplomacy and international summits alone. It also requires domestic institutions capable of providing legal continuity, budgetary support and public accountability.
Connectivity offers the clearest example. Kazakhstan has become central to efforts to expand the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, commonly known as the Middle Corridor. But transforming the corridor into a commercially competitive route requires more than diplomatic declarations. It depends on investment in railways, ports, logistics hubs and border infrastructure, as well as reforms to customs procedures, tariffs, digital documentation and public-private partnerships.
Many of these measures require legislation or long-term public expenditure. A parliament able to scrutinize infrastructure priorities, assess financing arrangements and monitor implementation can help turn regional connectivity from a collection of projects into a durable economic strategy. It can also provide greater continuity when individual ministers, officials or government programs change.
The same principle applies to trade and investment. Kazakhstan is seeking to diversify its economy while attracting capital into manufacturing, agriculture, transport, digital services and value-added processing. International investors generally look beyond headline agreements. They examine the stability of tax rules, the enforcement of contracts, customs administration, regulatory transparency and whether commitments will survive political cycles.
The new Kurultai will not determine the investment climate on its own. Nevertheless, its legislative and oversight functions can influence whether economic agreements produce predictable domestic rules. Parliamentary examination of budgets, taxation and sectoral legislation can also help identify gaps between international commitments and their implementation. This is particularly important for large infrastructure and industrial investments whose time horizons extend far beyond a single government program.
Energy and critical minerals present another area where domestic capacity and foreign policy increasingly intersect. Kazakhstan remains an important supplier of oil and uranium, while also seeking investment in renewable energy, electricity infrastructure, mineral processing and the production of materials required for the global energy transition.
International partnerships in these areas raise complex questions about environmental standards, infrastructure financing and the division of risks between the state and private investors. A more coherent legislative system could support a stable regulatory framework while ensuring that agreements contribute to economic diversification rather than simply expanding the export of unprocessed resources.
Water cooperation may offer the most difficult test. Central Asia’s major river systems cross national borders, while climate change, population growth and aging irrigation infrastructure are increasing pressure on available supplies. Regional agreements are essential, but their effectiveness depends on national decisions concerning agriculture, reservoirs, water pricing, infrastructure and environmental protection.
Parliamentary involvement can help connect regional negotiations with the domestic sectors and communities affected by them. It can also provide continuity for investments in water-saving technology and infrastructure that may require sustained funding over many years. In this sense, stronger domestic institutions are not an alternative to regional diplomacy; they are one of the conditions for making it effective.
The move from a bicameral parliament to the Kurultai is intended to create clearer political responsibility and a more streamlined legislative process. Having one chamber may reduce institutional overlap and make it easier for voters to identify which parties are responsible for legislative decisions. With all deputies elected through national party lists, the system may also encourage parties to develop programs addressing countrywide economic and social priorities.
The reforms may also give Kazakhstan’s foreign policy a broader domestic constituency. Its multivector approach has traditionally been guided primarily through presidential and professional diplomacy. A fully elected legislature creates another arena in which the principles underlying that approach, such as sovereignty, strategic autonomy, economic openness and cooperation with competing partners, can be articulated and debated. This matters in an environment where relations with Russia, China, the European Union and the United States intersect with supply-chain security and technological standards. Greater parliamentary involvement can make Kazakhstan’s international positioning more understandable at home and more resilient abroad, demonstrating that it rests on functioning institutions rather than executive preference alone.
The Kurultai can also strengthen parliamentary diplomacy. Relations between countries are shaped not only by governments and foreign ministries, but also through direct engagement between legislators, parliamentary friendship groups and interparliamentary organisations. Foreign lawmakers frequently influence decisions concerning trade preferences, export controls, investment financing, mobility arrangements and international agreements. Sustained engagement with them would provide Kazakhstan with an additional channel through which to explain its policies, address misunderstandings and develop constituencies supportive of cooperation. The foreign-policy benefit of the reform is therefore a broader institutional foundation for its established approach. This could reinforce the country’s reputation as a reliable middle power and make its international partnerships more resistant to political turnover and geopolitical shocks.
The election also includes mechanisms intended to broaden representation. Women, young people and persons with disabilities together account for more than two-fifths of registered candidates, while parties must meet a collective 30 percent quota for these groups both on their lists and when allocating mandates. Greater diversity cannot by itself guarantee legislative effectiveness, but it can widen the range of experience brought into debates over social policy, regional development and economic modernization.
Institutional design, however, does not automatically produce institutional capacity. The effectiveness of the Kurultai will depend on the quality of its committees, the policy expertise of its deputies, the ability of parties to develop distinguishable positions, and the seriousness with which oversight powers are exercised. A more efficient legislative process will be valuable only if efficiency is accompanied by substantive scrutiny. The significance of the election lies in the opportunity to establish a legislature with clearer responsibilities within Kazakhstan’s constitutional system.
The wider regional lesson is that Central Asia’s growing international agency needs to be matched by domestic institutions capable of implementing what governments negotiate abroad.
For that reason, the most important questions after the election will extend beyond which parties win seats. Attention should also be paid to how the Kurultai organizes its committees, uses its budgetary authority, oversees major projects and develops expertise on regional issues.
The election will provide an early indication of whether Kazakhstan can connect ambitious diplomacy with coherent legislative implementation. As the region seeks a larger role in Eurasian affairs, that connection will determine whether regional initiatives remain political declarations or become lasting institutions and infrastructure.

Liberia agrees to accept up to 1,200 third-country deportees from US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Liberia agrees to accept up to 1,200 third-country deportees from US
MONROVIA, Aug 18 - Liberia has agreed to accept up to 1,200 third-country deportees from the U.S. in the next 12 months, with an initial group of 20 deportees expected to arrive on Thursday, the government said in a statement on Tuesday.
Since taking office in January last year, the Trump administration has struck several deals with African countries on deporting people it cannot legally send to their home countries.
The deportees have in most cases obtained legal protection against repatriation after U.S. immigration judges ruled they risked torture or other abuses in their home countries.
Washington has defended the third-country deals as lawful, although rights groups and advocates have said the details are opaque and many of the deportees are ultimately repatriated.
The Liberian government's statement said the deportees "will include citizens or nationals of African and Western Hemisphere countries who are medically authorized to travel."
No information was immediately available on the nationalities of the deportees. The State Department said it does not disclose such details.
LIBERIA SAYS DEAL NOT 'A QUID PRO QUO'
Other African countries including the Democratic Republic of Congo, Central African Republic, Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon, Ghana and Sierra Leone have also accepted third-country deportees.
Liberia said on Tuesday that the deportees would be received "as guests" who could leave when they wanted and who could apply for asylum in Liberia.
The statement said the deal did not involve a quid pro quo with Washington and Monrovia was not demanding compensation for taking the deportees.
It added, however, that the government would receive "support to help manage the program and strengthen its migration system more broadly." It offered no further details.
The statement also referenced Liberia's history as a refuge for freed slaves from the U.S. and as a country with "a long history of accepting people seeking refuge from political and other crises."
President Joseph Boakai was one of five West African leaders who traveled to the White House last year to meet with Trump.
Reuters reported at the time that Trump had urged the leaders to accept third-country deportees. REUTERS

Iraqi armed factions begin to disarm as part of state plan to regulate weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
19:11:31 UTC
04:11:31 KST

Laith Al-Jnaidi and Mohammad Sio
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
Several factions operating under Iraq’s officially administered Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) have begun handing over their weapons as part of a government plan to place all arms under state control, an Iraqi security official said Tuesday.
Lieutenant-General Saad Maan, head of the Iraqi Security Media Cell, said several factions had already begun the process while others were moving in the same direction, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA).
According to Maan, the measures are part of institutional and legal arrangements aimed at regulating the status of armed formations – and their members – within the state military apparatus.
He said the initiative was aimed at strengthening the state’s authority and the rule of law, stressing that it was not aimed at any particular faction or group.
The policy applies to all weapons held outside official state institutions, regardless of who possesses them, including tribal weapons and arms not subject to existing laws and regulations, Maan said.
He also said that the PMF would “work to safeguard the rights of fighters from different factions and formations, as well as those of their families, in accordance with applicable laws and regulations.”
The PMF is an official security umbrella formed in 2014 after a religious ruling by Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani, a leading Iraqi Shia authority, which called for volunteers to fight the Daesh terrorist group.
In 2016, the PMF was formally incorporated into Iraq’s armed forces.
Maan denied that the government was preparing for a confrontation with armed factions.
“The Iraqi government is not in conflict with any formation or faction,” he said, adding that the issue was being handled as a constitutional and legal obligation related to Iraq’s security.
He stressed that placing weapons under state control “is not a project of confrontation, but one of state stability and community security.”
In June, Iraqi military spokesman Sabah al-Numan announced the establishment of a committee tasked with overseeing efforts to bring unregulated weapons under state control.
The issue remains one of Iraq’s most pressing political and security challenges, with some armed factions continuing to operate under the umbrella of the PMF while others operate independently.

What we do and don't know about guns in Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
19:11:30 UTC
04:11:30 KST

The number of firearms nationwide is significantly higher than before the Port Arthur massacre. But there's also a lot authorities can't tell us about just how many guns are out there.
The New South Wales government is aiming to remove more than 270,000 firearms from the community when its buyback scheme begins in November.
The "bigger than the Howard-era" scheme is part of legislation passed after the Bondi Beach terrorist attack in December last year.
But what do we really know about the number of guns in Australia? And who owns them?
4 million — The number of guns owned (legally) nationwide
Figures released by the Department of Home Affairs in January show there are a record number of firearms in Australia, with more than 4 million owned nationwide.
This equates to one firearm for every seven Australians.
Data from Home Affairs shows NSW has the most firearms, with more than 1.1 million, with Queensland a close second.
Tasmania and the Northern Territory have the highest per capita, with one firearm for every four people, according to a 2025 report from The Australia Institute.
25 per cent — The increase in guns since before Port Arthur
Despite significant gun reform following the Port Arthur massacre, Australia now has more firearms than before the mass shooting in 1996.
There are more than 4.1 million firearms in Australia, according to official data.
And that is up 25 per cent from the 3.2 million guns in Australia before Port Arthur, according to The Australia Institute.
After the mass shooting, then-prime minister John Howard announced a buyback scheme that saw more than 650,000 firearms destroyed.
A second national amnesty was launched in the months after the Lindt Cafe siege in 2017, when more than 57,000 items were handed in.
There were also several permanent and temporary amnesties in state and territory areas from 1996 to 2015.
In 2021, a permanent national gun amnesty was introduced, where anyone with an unregistered firearm could surrender it anonymously and without repercussions.
4.4 — The average number of guns for each owner
The Department of Home Affairs says there are more than 4 million firearms in Australia — 4,113,735 to be exact, according to January figures.
The department also confirms there are 929,741 firearms licences across the country.
That means each licensed gun owner has an average of 4.4 firearms.
And analysis from The Australia Institute suggests that number has increased over time.
"In NSW, that figure has risen from 4.0 per licence in 2016 to 4.5 in 2024; in Victoria the figure has risen from 3.6 in 2016 to 4.1 in 2024," the report says.
41 per cent — The proportion of gun owners in NSW who live in major cities
When we think about guns in Australia, there is general acceptance that people in rural and regional areas may need weapons for farming and pest control purposes.
But a large proportion of gun owners are in the city.
NSW publishes the most comprehensive and easily accessible data of any jurisdiction, including licence holders' postcodes.
The Australia Institute analysis found four in 10 NSW firearms licensees live in major cities.
And it's not an isolated case, with police in Western Australia saying 46 per cent of its firearms are located in metropolitan areas.
371 — The number of guns a single person owns in inner-city Sydney
NSW Police publish data on gun ownership twice a year, including the number of guns individuals own and their corresponding postcode.
In the latest release from December, the person with the highest number of guns had 371 firearms and lived in the 2090 postcode, which encompasses the affluent, harbourside suburb of Cremorne and its surrounds.
The data release lists the top 100 individuals by number of firearms owned — excluding collectors and dealers — with the lowest entry on the list owning 91 guns.
What are the gaps in our gun knowledge?
Gun reform researchers say there's a lot we don't know about gun ownership and how it relates to violent crime, especially due to the limited data available in jurisdictions other than NSW.
"New South Wales has quite a good registry, and quite a good repository of data, and some of the other states absolutely don't," gun violence researcher at the University of Sydney Joel Negin said.
"It presents challenges like information sharing between jurisdictions, and there was a high-profile case in Wieambilla where the individual was a licensed firearm holder in NSW, but the information wasn't available to Queensland in real time, and two police officers were killed."
Of course, that data would only track guns that have been legally obtained.
"One of the key questions that does get asked is of violent crime or of firearm-related crime, what percentage of that is perpetrated by licensed holders or by or with registered firearms," Dr Negin said.
"That's an important question that police forces around the country actually don't have a great answer to, and that's one of the topics that we're particularly interested in trying to understand a bit better."
Dr Negin believes there is a "narrative" that most registered firearm owners are law-abiding citizens and all crime comes from unlicensed holders or those with unregistered firearms.
"The truth is probably somewhere in between," he said.
"Bondi and the incident in western Queensland that I mentioned were all with registered firearms and licensed holders, so the narratives and the data are mixed and we don't have a great sense of it across the country."
'No idea' about illegal firearm numbers
Samara McPhedran has researched gun-related violence for 30 years and works with the Violence Prevention Institute of Australia.
She said changes to the National Firearms Register (NFR) and the new buyback scheme won't prevent future gun violence because of the illegal weapons in the community that go untracked.
"We have research that is really clear that the number of legally owned guns does not relate to the level of firearm crime or violence," she said.
"By its very nature, the illegal ownership of firearms is largely invisible, we have no idea what the numbers out there really look like.
"Even numbers collected by arrests would be the tip of the iceberg."
The last major estimate from the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission was in 2023, when it made a conservative estimate that there were about 200,000 illegally obtained or manufactured weapons in Australia.
The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime advises that a country can estimate the number of illegal firearms as 10 to 20 per cent of the number of registered firearms.
"So if you did that in Australia, and again, these are rough estimates, but if you did that in Australia, you'd fall somewhere between 300,000 and 600,000 illegal firearms," Deakin University criminologist and forensic psychologist David Bright said.
These weapons, he said, likely entered the black market through theft, illegal importation and owners not surrendering them during amnesties.
3D-printed guns emerge as 'game changer'
The emergence of 3D-printed guns and gun parts presents a rising challenge.
"People can now make these weapons in suburban homes and they're just as good as a factory-made firearm and you couldn't say that five or ten years ago," Professor Bright said.
"The concern is people can get their hands on a working firearm in an extremely covert manner and we just don't have the policy or regulatory frameworks to actually deal with this problem."
In June, it was revealed one person was being charged every fortnight in Queensland alone with possessing a blueprint to make 3D-printed guns.
Dr McPhedran said evidence showed the ways people were obtaining illegal weapons had changed.
"Even though legal gun ownership has gone up, theft has gone down so that has changed the pathway in terms of how people are illegally obtaining firearms.
"3D printing has really been a game changer in terms of criminal acquisition of firearms."
With so many illegal weapons out there, she said federal changes to the NFR and buyback schemes were "purely symbolic" in terms of reducing the risk of gun violence.
"What's unfortunately happened, and we've seen this again after Bondi, is there will be a high-profile incident involving firearms, and then a very swift reaction from politicians to crack down on legal ownership.
"That is at odds with what the evidence tells us, which is that those illegally owned firearms … are the ones that are the highest risk because they are in the hands of people who are the highest risk."
Professor Bright said cooperation across all states was also essential to effective gun control.
About the data
- The Australia Institute report states that because data on firearms is not published consistently across states and territories, and there is no publicly available national database, its reporting aggregates data from various government sources, including state police force annual reports and third-party sources such as GunPolicy.org.

US judge says government can revoke deportation protections for Ethiopians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
19:09:23 UTC
04:09:23 KST

US judge says government can revoke deportation protections for Ethiopians
Ruling permits Trump administration to nix Temporary Protected Status for Ethiopians despite concerns over conditions in their home country.
A United States federal judge has ruled that the administration of President Donald Trump can revoke legal protections that shielded more than 5,000 Ethiopians from deportation.
On Tuesday, US District Judge Brian Murphy gave the go-ahead for the termination of the group’s Temporary Protected Status (TPS), a legal category that allows foreign nationals in the US to stay and apply for work authorisation, on the basis that conditions in their home country may not be safe to return to.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Will the end of TPS for Haitians mean a caregiving crisis in US?
- list 2 of 3US judge blocks Trump bid to strip work permits from immigrants
- list 3 of 3US courts clear way for deportations of South Sudan, Myanmar nationals
Since returning to office for a second term in 2025, Trump has sought to end TPS protections for a range of nationalities.
Tuesday’s ruling removes the final judicial block that had prevented the government from ending TPS for individual countries. Administration officials celebrated the ruling.
“Judge Brian Murphy just lifted the stay of Ethiopia TPS termination,” Department of Homeland Security General Counsel James Percival wrote in a social media post. “All TPS terminations are in effect!”
The decision follows a 6-3 ruling from the US Supreme Court in June that limited the ability of courts to review Homeland Security’s efforts to terminate TPS protections.
While the Supreme Court’s ruling focused on TPS recipients from Syria and Haiti, it also had broader applications for people of other nationalities fighting the premature termination of their TPS status.
Roughly 1.29 million people were living in the US under the protection of the TPS system as of March. They represented 17 countries where the US government had deemed conditions unsafe or unstable.
The Trump administration, however, has sought to terminate TPS protections for at least 13 of those nationalities, including people from Venezuela, Nicaragua, South Sudan and Somalia.
The Pew Research Center estimates that the TPS revocations will affect at least one million people who were participating in the programme as of this year.
Trump has undertaken a large-scale effort to restrict immigration and increase deportations since embarking on his second term. Revoking TPS has been part of that project.
His administration has argued that repeated extensions to the TPS programme have rendered it less a “temporary” programme and more a long-term one.
“Temporary Protected Status is just that — TEMPORARY,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote on Tuesday, in reaction to the latest ruling.
He then issued a warning to those who found their legal status cancelled: “If you are in our nation and your status has been terminated, you are here ILLEGALLY. You have two options: leave immediately or be swiftly deported.”
But critics have pointed out that TPS is being revoked for groups whose home countries continue to suffer from civil conflict, natural disasters, and other dangers.
Ethiopians living in the US were first granted TPS under the administration of former President Joe Biden in 2022 over concerns about violent conflict and humanitarian issues in Ethiopia.
The US State Department currently lists the country under a level-three travel advisory on its four-point scale, advising citizens not to travel there due to “unrest, crime, kidnapping, terrorism [and] landmines”.
The Department of Homeland Security first announced in December that it would end TPS protections for Ethiopians, stating that conditions in the country “no longer pose a serious threat to the personal safety of returning Ethiopian nationals”.
Rights groups, however, have pointed out that the Trump administration’s decision does not appear to reflect the reality on the ground in Ethiopia.
“The crisis in Ethiopia is still ongoing, and this decision puts the lives of thousands of Ethiopians living in the US at severe risk,” Diana Konate, deputy executive director of policy and advocacy at the group African Communities Together, told the news agency Reuters.
Judge Murphy had previously paused the Trump administration’s attempts to end TPS for Ethiopians, as he considered issues not addressed by the Supreme Court’s June decision.
His court heard arguments that it was the attorney general, not the Department of Homeland Security, that was empowered under the law to end TPS protections before their expiry.
But ultimately, Murphy dismissed that argument — though Tuesday’s decision leaves open the possibility of an appeal on the basis that the Trump administration was motivated in its decision by animus against certain races or nationalities.

A government-owned ferry that capsized on Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba last week was carrying about 180 passengers, double what police had given as its capacity, the government said on Tuesday, as the death toll rose to 94.
State-controlled newspaper The Herald said it was the deadliest transport disaster in the Southern African country's history, surpassing a 1991 bus crash that claimed 89 lives.
The boat was travelling from the town of Kariba in northern Zimbabwe to a remote rural community on the lake when it capsized after being struck by strong waves.
The ferry was only meant to carry 90 passengers, police said last week. While the government statement did not say the maximum number that should have been on board, it said the 180 passengers and goods exceeded “its carrying capacity”.
Police on Tuesday put the death toll, which has risen steadily over the week since the capsize, at 94.
Some 77 people have been rescued so far, while search and recovery operations continue, the government said in the statement released after a Cabinet meeting.
Lake Kariba, on the border between Zimbabwe and Zambia, is one of the world's largest man-made reservoirs.

Temporary visa rules leave Iranian refugee 'trapped in nightmare'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
19:04:01 UTC
04:04:01 KST

Iranian refugee fears temporary visa could lead to separation from family
Mahsa Mazaheri wakes up every day feeling like she is "trapped in a nightmare" and fearing she will be separated from her husband and two daughters at any time.
For the past eight years, the Iranian refugee has had to reapply for a temporary bridging visa to stay in Australia, which expires every six months.
"I'm scared. I have to remind myself, 'Don't forget to check the date. Don't forget,'" Ms Mazaheri told the ABC.
Ms Mazaheri and her mother came to Australia from Iran by boat in 2013 and were sent to offshore detention centres on Naoero (formerly Nauru) and Christmas Island.
Their time in those facilities felt like "time in jail", but the pair were medically evacuated to mainland Australia after her mother's health worsened in 2014.
They have been in visa limbo since.
Under Australia's immigration policies for people who arrived by boat, Ms Mazaheri and her mother have been denied any pathway to a permanent visa in Australia.
They are part of a cohort of more than 700 survivors of offshore detention living in Australia with no permanency, according to the Human Rights Law Centre.
Despite their uncertain visa status, many have started families, had children, and built lives they say they cannot leave behind.
Ms Mazaheri is a small-business owner who pays taxes, but she cannot leave the country or make long-term plans because of restrictions on her temporary visa.
Lives built around 'insecure visas'
Human Rights Law Centre associate legal director Laura John said that under the Australian government's migration laws, people previously held in offshore detention who were now living in Australia are categorised as "transitory persons".
"Despite living in Australia for over a decade, having an Australian citizen partner or children, working in critical industries and being part of the fabric of the Australian community, the 700 people previously held in offshore detention who have built homes in Australia are still left on short-term, insecure visas," she said.
Ms Mazaheri said reapplying for her visa every three or six months, with no guarantee it would be granted, had been emotionally taxing.
"I'm not sure if they give me the visa or they tell me I have to go to a different country," she said.
"We don't know what's going to happen the next day."
Ms John, who has been working closely with Ms Mazaheri and her family, said Australia's offshore processing policy had "caused immeasurable harm to thousands of people and their families".
Ms John said it was time the government abandoned "cruel and senseless policies from the past" and let people stay with their families and communities.
"Transitory persons temporarily residing in Australia under regional processing arrangements do not have a permanent settlement pathway in Australia," a Department of Home Affairs spokesperson said
"Transitory persons are encouraged to consider their options to depart Australia, either to a third country or return to their home country.
"A range of support is available to transitory persons to connect with third country migration options or to return home voluntarily."
'I just want permanent safety'
Ms Mazaheri has set up a life with her husband, whom she met in Australia, and their two daughters, who are four and three years of age.
"We have the kids, we have a family, and I just want permanent safety," she said.
Ms Mazaheri's husband arrived by boat from Iran a few days after her, but was not transferred to Naoero because the government's policy "was not applied consistently", according to Ms John.
Ms Mazaheri's husband was allowed to apply for refugee protection onshore and was granted Australian citizenship earlier this year.
Their two daughters were added to their father's application, and both are now Australian citizens.
It was a bittersweet outcome for Ms Mazaheri.
"I was really happy for them, but in my heart I was really upset," she said.
Ms Mazaheri said the situation reminded her of the possibility of being taken from her daughters due to her temporary status.
"In Iran I had a really hard situation with the government, but here it's harder for me," she said.
"Every morning when I wake up, I'm thinking about my kids: 'Am I going to stay with them? Maybe the Australian government is going to surprise me. If they tell me to go to a different country, what should I do?'
"I don't have any future now."
The bridging visa Ms Mazaheri and her mother have been granted includes conditions such as limitations on work and study, and they are subject to a conduct of behaviour policy, according to the Department of Immigration.
The website states that Bridging Visa E (BVE) has two categories: subclasses 051 and 050.
Both BVE categories are described as temporary visas that "let you stay lawfully in Australia" while you wait for an immigration decision or for your protection visa to be processed.
People on BVEs have to reapply for Medicare benefits every time their visas expire.
Ms Mazaheri said that she had gone without Medicare cover many times while waiting for a pending application, which could sometimes take up to three months.
That has meant that her mother, whom Ms Mazaheri cares for full-time, has gone without medical treatment due to the high out-of-pocket fees.
"My daughter, she asks, 'Oh, mummy, can we go on holiday back to see grandma?' But it's too hard to sit down and explain to a four-year-old, 'Oh, mummy can't because I don't have a visa,'" Ms Mazaheri said.
Ms Mazaheri's case is among a large number of individual cases submitted to Immigration Minister Tony Burke, according to Ms John.
"If the minister decided not to grant a bridging visa, a person could be ripped from their family, taken into immigration detention and sent back to Nauru [Naoero] or potentially deported to their country of origin," she said.
"Our migration laws prevent people in this group from applying for any permanent visa, including a partner visa, unless Minister Burke personally intervenes in their case. Without a permanent visa, people are not eligible for Australian citizenship."
Ms John said the roughly 700 refugees had very few protections to prevent deportation back to the country they fled from.
"Even to a place like Iran," she said.
"Minister Burke already has the power to grant permanent safety to Mahsa and the other 700 people who are trapped in limbo.
"It is time for people to be given the protection they first sought over 13 years ago. Granting people permanent safety will simply reflect the practical reality that Australia is now their home."
The Human Rights Law Centre, Asylum Seeker Resource Centre and advocacy group GetUp are petitioning Mr Burke to grant permanent residency to the refugees in limbo.

EU facing food crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
19:02:07 UTC
04:02:07 KST

EU facing food crisis
Agricultural producers across the EU have warned of sharp drops in yields after Europe has been hit by successive heatwaves this summer. Economists have said the losses are likely to push food prices higher in the coming months.
June and July were the hottest on record in western Europe, according to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, which has warned of a “continued risk of heatwaves affecting much of Europe” through August and into September.
In France, one of the EU’s largest grain producers, groundwater reserves were severely depleted across much of the country by early August, according to the national geological survey.
Prince de Bretagne, a major growers’ cooperative in Brittany, warned last week of a “historic” vegetable crisis. It projected yield declines of 40% for peas, 60% for broccoli, and between 50% and 100% for artichokes this summer.
Eric Legras, president of Unilet, France’s leading association of canned and frozen vegetable producers, said severe heat had also hit northern and southwestern France, describing the crisis as “exceptional.”
Livestock farmers have meanwhile warned of a growing “forage production deficit” ahead of winter. France’s National Committee for the Promotion of Eggs has estimated that heatwaves have cut daily output by around one million eggs, while poultry farms have reported high mortality rates.
In northern Italy, home to one of Europe’s main rice-growing regions, water shortages have left some paddies “completely dead, burnt, with the rice dried out,” according to Coldiretti, the country’s largest farmers’ association.
Farmers in Spain have likewise reported considerable shortfalls in cereal yields, as well as cattle fodder deficits.
The German Farmers’ Association on Tuesday warned that grain production would be 7%, or 3.3 million tons, lower than last year. The worst-hit regions in the south of the country could potentially suffer total crop failures.
In neighboring Poland, business outlet Puls Biznesu predicted last month that persistent drought could force the country to become more reliant on food imports.
Analysts at Zurich Insurance Group and several European banks have estimated that the heatwaves could cost the EU between €50 billion and €180 billion.

Rising US debt threatens to drive up household, business borrowing costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
19:01:58 UTC
04:01:58 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
The US national debt has surpassed $39 trillion, threatening to raise borrowing costs for households and businesses while placing growing pressure on federal retirement programs, according to a report released Tuesday by the Conference Board.
The debt now amounts to approximately $116,000 per American, based on the US population as of July 2026, the nonprofit business research group said in its report, How the National Debt Affects All Generations of Americans.
The study modeled five fiscal scenarios and examined how changes in deficits, interest rates and financial stability could affect students financing their education, families purchasing homes, retirees relying on Social Security and small-business owners seeking funding.
It found that reducing budget deficits could lower borrowing costs and improve the country’s fiscal outlook, while larger deficits and financial shocks could significantly increase the cost of student loans, mortgages and business financing.
Under a scenario involving a weeklong US debt default, small-business loan payments could increase by 21.6%, modeled student-loan costs by 8.7% and housing costs by as much as 6.7%, the report said.
“The national debt is not just a number on the government’s balance sheet — it affects the financial decisions Americans make every day,” said David Young, president of the Conference Board’s CEO Center.
Higher debt could mean higher borrowing costs, fewer resources for national priorities and greater uncertainty surrounding retirement programs, he added.
The report projects the national debt will reach 154% of gross domestic product by 2036 under its baseline scenario and 180% under a higher-deficit scenario.
It also warned that the main trust fund used to pay Social Security retirement benefits is projected to become insolvent in 2032.
If Congress allows benefits to fall to the amount supported by incoming program revenue, retirees could face a 7% benefit cut in 2032 and average annual reductions of 28% between 2033 and 2036, according to projections cited in the report.
Alternatively, maintaining scheduled benefits through transfers from the Treasury’s general fund would require an estimated $2.7 trillion between 2032 and 2036, potentially adding further to federal deficits.
The Conference Board called for a bipartisan congressional fiscal commission, comprehensive Social Security reforms, modernization of Medicare and improvements to the federal budget process.

Is US weighing smaller Gulf troop footprint as Iran absorbs attacks and strikes back freely?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
19:00:19 UTC
04:00:19 KST

When the US and Israel joined forces to attack Iran on February 28, Washington initially stated that the war with Iran was projected to last four to six weeks.
Iran immediately responded to the US-Israeli attacks — that killed the longtime supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and much of the other top brass as well as hundreds of civilians — by asserting presence in the Strait of Hormuz and conducting missile and drone strikes across the Gulf, impacting global stability.
As US military strikes on Iran continued, Washington frequently shifted the goalpost and timeline, claiming it was "ahead of schedule" and later stating it would last an additional two to three weeks or continue "as long as necessary".
Now, five months and 21 days later, the war — although at a low intensity — continues despite repeated ceasefire attempts.
With around 18 confirmed US military deaths and roughly 600–900 personnel wounded, as well as significant aircraft and equipment losses — notably dozens of drones and several fighter jets and tankers — in the ongoing Operation Epic Fury, official US war costs are estimated to reach $37.5 billion by the end of September 2026.
Attacks by Iran have involved missiles, drones, and other munitions. While many were intercepted, satellite imagery, official statements, and reports confirm damage to infrastructure and equipment, including radar systems, air defence installations, hangars, fuel depots, aircraft, and communications networks in host countries.
According to The Washington Post, the damage caused to US bases and assets by Iran has also offered a rare opportunity to reconsider the US military posture in the region, with officials indicating that some bases may not be rebuilt in their previous form.
Citing eight people familiar with the matter, The Post reported on Tuesday that Pentagon is reassessing its military footprint in the Middle East, signalling that the war on Iran could potentially reshape the US presence in the region.
The US news outlet added that one of the key areas the Defense Department is assessing is whether to pull back troops from the Gulf, "where America's large overseas military bases have been battered by months of Iranian strikes."
The review is being led by the Pentagon's policy office, alongside assessments by the Joint Staff and US Central Command, according to the report.
A senior Pentagon official told The Washington Post that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had not ordered a formal review, describing the move as "prudent planning" to guide decisions on rebuilding damaged bases.
"Decisions are going to have to be made on some of this stuff," the official said.
40,000 troops at 20 sites
US Central Command typically maintains about 40,000 troops at nearly 20 sites stretching from Jordan to Oman.
Since early this year, Washington has deployed additional warships, fighter aircraft and air defence systems to the region and carried out more than 13,000 attacks on Iran.
The largest permanent US bases in the region are concentrated in the Gulf, including the Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain and major Army and Air Force facilities in countries such as Kuwait.
While Iran and the US signed the memorandum of understanding in June through Pakistani and Qatari mediation, ending hostilities and opening a 60-day window for negotiations toward a final agreement, missiles and drones continue to fly over the region. 
Talks have since stalled amid disputes over implementation of the memorandum and arrangements for navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil and gas exports.
"People familiar with the Pentagon's analysis said the issue is likely to intensify a debate between camps within the administration that support military interventions and others that have argued the Pentagon should curtail some of its security commitments to refocus on defending the US homeland or deterring more powerful adversaries, like China," The Post added.
The discussions have also involved Admiral Bradley Cooper, the head of US Central Command, who supports deliberations about potentially moving US troops west from the Gulf, a US official told the news outlet.
"The war really did highlight the vulnerability ... of US forces in the region," Michael Ratney, a former diplomat who served as the US envoy to Saudi Arabia and the deputy chief of mission in Qatar, told The Washington Post.
He argued that redeploying troops and equipment west towards Jordan, Israel, or Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast could ease pressure, though noting the extra distance was not a "perfect solution to this problem."

IN BRIEF: Remains of Holy Right-Believing Grand Prince Dmitry Donskoy discovered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:59:03 UTC
03:59:03 KST

MOSCOW, August 18. /TASS/. The remains of the Holy Right-Believing Grand Prince Dmitry Donskoy have been discovered during restoration works in the Kremlin’s Cathedral of the Archangel.
A combined study has proven their authenticity. Their fragments will be placed for worship in churches of the Russian Orthodox Church.
Below are key facts about the discovery.
Discovery of remains
- Restoration efforts were carried out in July 2026 to fix the subsidence of floor slabs that threatened to destroy tomb monuments.
- In order to facilitate the removal of the floor slabs, brick tomb monuments of a crypt near the southern wall of the cathedral were dismantled.
- The restoration effort led to the discovery of three solid white-stone sarcophagi.
- They were identified as belonging to Holy Right-Believing Grand Prince Dmitry Ivanovich Donskoy, Grand Prince Ivan II Ivanovich the Fair, and Prince Dmitry Ivanovich Zhilka of Uglich.
Authenticity of remains and their state
- A combination of historical data, of the burial site’s archaeological context and the results of an anthropological study have confirmed the authenticity of the remains, a source in the Russian Orthodox Church has told TASS.
- The remains were intact in the sarcophagus apart from the left heel bone.
- The bones show no signs of postmortem damage and are well preserved.
Worship of believers
- With the blessing of Patriarch Kirill of Moscow and All Russia, parts of the remains will be placed in different Russian Orthodox churches, the source told TASS.
Condition of sarcophagus
- The lid of the sarcophagus was damaged, the Russian Orthodox Church source has told TASS.
- During the visual inspection, specialists discovered two transverse cracks in the lid, and its middle section was at risk of collapsing inside the sarcophagus, which would have resulted in damage or destruction of the holy remains.
- Museum curators received the blessing of Patriarch of Moscow and All Russia Kirill to carry out emergency stabilization and restoration works.
- Information about the position of the sarcophagi came as news to curators of the Moscow Kremlin Museums, the source said.
- Based on the available data about the burial sites, engineers had to place Dmitry Donskoy’s sarcophagus under that of Ivan the Fair in order to free up space for utility lines.
- In the 1860s, the sarcophagi of Dmitry Donskoy and Ivan Krasny had to be raised to the floor level, above their burial pits.
Prayer service near the remains
- Patriarch of Moscow and All Russia Kirill led a prayer service near the uncovered remains, a TASS correspondent reported.
- He was assisted by Metropolitan Grigory of Voskresensk and the Bishop of Ramenskoye.

Israeli teen’s IOI gold medal revoked after displaying Israeli flag at awards ceremony
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:56:58 UTC
03:56:58 KST

A 17-year-old Israeli student had his gold medal win disqualified at the 2026 International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) in Uzbekistan, after wearing the Israeli flag during the awards ceremony.
Yotam Budnik, from Rehovot, raised the flag during the live-broadcast TV ceremony, despite knowing that Israeli symbols were not allowed.
Since October 7, IOI hosts have forbidden Israeli contestants from competing with national symbols. As a result, the education minister advised against sending a team. This year, however, it was agreed the students would go as independent contestants, without representing Israel specifically.
Team leader Ron Ryvchin told The Jerusalem Post on Tuesday that despite the rules, “Yotam basically felt that this entire situation is quite absurd because the decision to forbid us from showing the flag was accepted without us being able to defend ourselves.
“Even in 2024, we competed online, and then they erased the name of Israel from the ceremonies. They even erased the name of Israel from the map, and they did not mention our online contestants at all.
“So he felt, year after year, Israeli students are erased from their national identity or even erased completely. So he decided that as an act of protest, he wouldn’t follow this rule. He showed the flag on the stage.”
Afterward, the international committee disqualified him because he did not follow the rule.
Yotam refused to hand over medal until teammates received theirs
The president of the IOI went to Yotam to take his medal, but he “refused to hand it over” until his friends received their medals.
“He was really, really, really brave. It was amazing to see a 17-year-old boy talking so well to them. He told them this rule is nonsense and that they just discriminate against people based on their country. And that he thinks that in an organization that should be focused on informatics and on bringing people together from various nations, fostering friendships, there is no place for these politics.”
According to Ryvchin, the organizers told Yotam that he still must follow the rules.
“They said that he made the first mistake when he showed the flag, and now he’s making the second one, that it’s better for him to return [the medal].”
They then removed him from the international IOI website, and he no longer appears in the ranking.
“They changed his score to zero. So, like officially, he’s not an IOI gold medalist.
“But, of course, we all think he earned his medal by himself. He worked very hard; he’s super talented. I think he deserves this medal.”
Ryvchin: 'Really great' competition despite incident, Israelis win four medals
Aside from this incident, Ryvchin said the competition “was really great,” and three Israeli students won gold, and one bronze.
“It was the first IOI for everyone. So it really is very impressive because it’s very difficult in the first competition under pressure to perform so well.”
He told the Post he hopes the IOI will realize that the best way to really foster friendship and encourage young students everywhere to study informatics “is to leave the politics out because it’s kind of absurd.”
Mostly, he wanted to congratulate the “amazing Israeli students” again, who didn’t even know in advance they would participate, but trained really hard anyway.
“I’m really proud of them,” he said.

Trump administration moves ahead to end roadless rule on national forests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:53:02 UTC
03:53:02 KST

Trump administration moves ahead to end roadless rule on national forests
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (AP) — The Trump administration announced Tuesday it is moving ahead with plans to rescind a quarter-century-old rule that blocked logging, road building and other development on national forest lands, drawing the ire of environmentalists nationwide.
The U.S. Forest Service is filing a proposal that would scrap the so called roadless rule adopted in the last days of Bill Clinton’s presidency in 2001. The agency described the rule as a one-size-fits-all restriction that has frustrated land managers and served as a barrier to reducing wildfire risks in the nation’s forests.
“Our forests can’t afford another decade of inaction. Across the country, we’ve watched preventable conditions — overgrown stands, insect outbreaks and disease — turn healthy landscapes into tinderboxes,” U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said in a statement.
Scientists say that worsening wildfires are driven by a combination of climate change that warms and dries out forests, less logging and decades of fire suppression that has allowed fuels to build up.
Clinton had signed the rule to safeguard undeveloped national forest land from commercial logging and mineral leasing, with a goal of keeping ecosystems pristine and protecting water supplies.
Calling the roadless rule a failure, Rollins said the proposal calls for restoring authority to local forest managers and removing barriers that have kept them from improving forest health across millions of acres.
The roadless rule has affected 30% of national forest lands nationwide, or about 59 million acres (24 million hectares), according to the Department of Agriculture, the agency over the Forest Service.
The Forest Service will gather public comment on the proposal and on a draft of the environmental impact statement that was filed Tuesday in the Federal Register. While the rescission removes national designation of roadless areas, officials say it doesn’t mandate timber cutting or road construction.
The filing comes as no surprise as the Trump administration first announced its intention to get rid of the rule during a meeting last summer in New Mexico.
Environmentalists have been sounding the alarm since then and reiterated Tuesday that lifting protections would have detrimental effects for old growth forests, wildlife and water supplies.
“Americans across the political spectrum have made it crystal clear that they don’t want political appointees removing protections from public lands,” said Chris Krupp, an attorney with the group WildEarth Guardians. “It would be a gross misreading of public sentiment to take the roadless rule away from Americans and our wildlife, and politicians do so at their jeopardy.”
Numerous groups raised concerns about what a rescission could mean, especially for places such as Alaska’s Tongass National Forest, the nation’s largest national forest and a lightning rod for litigation. State political leaders there have supported an exemption to the roadless rule that they argue impedes economic opportunities.
During the latter part of Trump’s first term, the federal government lifted restrictions on logging and road-building in the Tongass, something the Biden administration later reversed.
Emma Powell, the Alaska Wilderness League’s government affairs manager, described the Tongass as a global treasure that serves as a home for salmon runs and abundant wildlife. She added that cultures and livelihoods are connected to the forest.
“From fisheries to tourism and outdoor recreation, these landscapes also support thousands of jobs and generate billions in economic activity each year,” Powell said.
Alex Craven, the Sierra Club’s forest campaign manager, disputed officials’ claims that getting rid of the rule would allow for more work to be done to reduce wildfire threats. Craven suggested more roads would lead to more fires and that it never prevented the Forest Service from doing targeted work to reduce wildfire fuels.
He vowed that the Sierra Club and other groups would fight the proposal at each step.
David Jenkins, president of the Virginia-based nonprofit Conservatives for Responsible Stewardship, criticized the proposal as fiscally irresponsible and pointed to an existing maintenance backlog that stretches into the billions of dollars.
“The agency doesn’t have the budget to take care of the 368,000 miles of roads already riddling our national forests,” he said.
The deadline for comments is Sept. 21.

Gambling red flag system under fire as 'Dracula in charge'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:52:04 UTC
03:52:04 KST

Gambling reforms put onus on bookies to flag vulnerable punters
In short:
Wagering companies will have to identify customers showing signs of problem gambling and stop sending them betting inducements.
Critics say allowing the industry to flag its own vulnerable users is too weak, but the federal government says it will curb predatory tactics.
What's next?
Labor's gambling reforms are expected to pass the Senate with the support of the Coalition this week, with detailed criteria of the new red flag inducement system to be developed in the coming months.
Australian wagering companies will identify their own problem gamblers and cut off betting inducements under a system one critic has likened to putting "Dracula in charge of a blood bank".
The plan to let the industry red flag its own vulnerable customers has been labelled weak by advocates who wanted tougher restrictions on the "predatory" tactics, while supporters have described the measure as "significant" reform.
The federal government's gambling ad crackdown passed the lower house on Tuesday and is expected to pass the Senate before the parliament sitting week ends after Labor struck a deal with the Coalition.
Following harrowing evidence about gambling addicts being offered bonus bets and other incentives to gamble being heard at a parliamentary inquiry, the government agreed to curtail so-called inducements.
This included an amendment to create a red flag system where companies are required to tag customers showing signs of problem gambling and stop sending promotions to those individuals.
Liberal MP Andrew Wallace, who was one of two Coalition members to cross the floor and vote against the bill over concerns it was not strong enough, said he did not trust gambling companies to flag potentially lucrative customers.
"I don't think it's acceptable that the bill basically gives [companies] the power to determine whether someone is a problem gambler or not," he said.
"To me, that's like putting Dracula in charge of a blood bank."
In the coming months, existing evidence and research about gambling, such as spend amount, frequency or other betting patterns, will be used to create metrics to guide companies on who they must flag.
Further details like transparency requirements and whether the red flag would be time-limited would also be finalised.
The government would impose the red flag scheme through regulation, with the Australian Media Communications Authority (ACMA) responsible for its enforcement and handling complaints.
Currently, gambling companies are required to identify and respond appropriately to problem behaviour through state and territory regulation, but the national laws would specifically link this work to inducements.
Further restrictions on inducements and TV ads
Further agreed amendments stop companies from marketing inducements to new customers for 14 days from account sign-up, and for three months to people who have come off the self-exclusion register Betstop.
The bill also now bans wagering staff from earning commissions based on customers' gambling activity.
Tackling inducements became a major focus of amendment talks after a Senate inquiry this month heard allegations from NRL player Luke Bateman that gambling company employees unofficially offered to arrange illicit drugs while cultivating relationships with him as a high-volume punter.
The issue was also included in Labor's 2026 national platform endorsed at the party's conference in July.
This week, Labor also agreed to amendments put forward by the Coalition to establish a new opt-out register for gambling advertising, to be called Adstop.
Further changes were also made to extend the ad blackout on television to at least 15 minutes before a live sport game, mirror the broadcast restrictions for streaming platforms and ban ads during children's programming.
The ABC revealed on Monday the gambling agreement had been reached before it was finalised on Tuesday morning with the endorsement of the full Labor caucus and all but a handful of Coalition party room members.
'Incredibly disappointing', says MP who crossed floor
Along with Mr Wallace, Nationals MP Pat Conaghan argued the laws did not go far enough and broke ranks to vote against the gambling bills in the House of Representatives.
Coalition backbenchers are permitted to cross the floor when in opposition if they inform colleagues of their intent, with at least one senator also reserving their right to do the same.
Mr Conaghan, who was on the committee for the online gambling harm inquiry chaired by late Labor MP Peta Murphy three years ago, said it was "incredibly disappointing" many of the recommendations from that report had been "discarded".
"It would have been great to see a national regulator … and to get rid of those inducements online where we heard that evidence from family members of loved ones who had taken their own lives because of the shame and debt," he told Afternoon Briefing.
"I do not live in a bubble; I know it wouldn't have been all 31 recommendations, but the major ones should have been put through.
"Peta Murphy would be incredibly disappointed, and exactly why I crossed the floor for the first time in my career."
Greens say reforms are 'riddled' with holes
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese heralded the legislation as the "most significant gambling advertising reform by any Australian government ever".
"It increases protections for people most at risk of gambling harm, while continuing to allow those who enjoy a bet to do so," he said.
Communications Minister Anika Wells said Labor had listened to a "range of views" across the community and parliament and decided to tackle the "most toxic version" of gambling inducements.
"This package of reforms minimises children's exposure to wagering advertising, takes action on predatory inducements and cracks down on illegal gambling operators," she said.
Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson said the Coalition had negotiated tougher protections where they were needed, while ensuring the laws were "practical, proportionate and respect personal responsibility".
"The Coalition has secured stronger rules around live sport online, children's programs, predatory inducements and the illegal gambling ads flooding social media," she said.
But Greens communications spokeswoman Sarah Hanson-Young said the gambling legislation was "riddled with holes" and criticised Opposition Leader Angus Taylor for making a deal with Mr Albanese.
"The whole bill is a dog, and it's now become a dog's breakfast," she said.
"Angus Taylor has been weak. He's rolled over, and he's yapping like Toto the dog.
"Let's be clear: this is not reform. This is a protection racket for an industry that has lost its social license."
Gambling industry says 'devil will be in the detail'
Responsible Wagering Australia (RWA), a peak industry body for licensed gambling companies, was critical of the amendments made to the bill this week and argued the changes disregard the risk of pushing gamblers to unregulated offshore markets.
RWA chief executive Kai Cantwell said there must be scrutiny of measures that added cost and complexity without a "clear link" to reducing harm.
"The devil will be in the detail, expected to largely be left to regulation."
Mr Cantwell said the complexities of the opt-out advertising register risked undermining the self-exclusion service Betstop and created "serious" implementation concerns.
He said Betstop had taken more than four years to fully implement and questioned how a similar version for all online advertising could be achieved in only four months.
The gambling bill is due to take effect from January 1 next year, but the government is anticipating the Adstop register would take longer to establish
Mr Cantwell said overall the new measures would "significantly curtail" Australian companies' ability to "advertise a legal product safely to adults".
"If you push people away from the licensed, regulated market — by banning or limiting the promotions that let local operators compete, or by making Australian odds less competitive with new taxes and levies — you don't stop them punting," he said.
"You push them offshore, into products with no consumer protections, no support, no Betstop, and no contribution to Australian sport and racing."

Trump administration to rescind rule protecting old-growth forests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:51:47 UTC
03:51:47 KST

The Trump administration said on Tuesday it plans to rescind the “roadless rule” that has protected old-growth forests in the US for 25 years, potentially opening up almost 45m acres of national forests to road construction, drilling and logging.
Conservationists had feared the announcement was coming since last summer after Brooke Rollins, Trump’s secretary of agriculture, targeted a rule brought in by Bill Clinton’s administration, describing it as “overly restrictive” and an “absurd obstacle” to development.
On Tuesday the US Forest Service, an agency inside the Department of Agriculture, formally announced it had filed the proposal to rescind in its entirety the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.
Environmental groups immediately criticized the plan for rollbacks of protections to forests from Alaska to Oregon to North Carolina.
“[The rule] is the only thing preventing much of our wildest remaining national forests from industrial development. These forests offer critical habitat for wildlife, provide clean, fresh air and water for millions and contain vast swathes of the last remaining old-growth forests in the country,” said Alex Craven, forest campaign manager for the Sierra Club.
The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) appealed for submissions for the public comment period to “defend our forests from the administration’s chopping block”.
“Their scheme would open up tens of millions of acres of our national forests to destructive logging, drilling and road building – including iconic public lands from California’s Tahoe national forest to Alaska’s Tongass national forest to the Appalachian Trail,” the NRDC said.
The Trump administration said the move would remove obstacles to managing forests and fighting wildfires.
Rollins said: “For too long, outdated restrictions have kept tens of millions of forested acres off-limits to the very treatments that improve forest health and reduce wildfire risk to our communities.
“Today, we filed a proposal to restore authority to local forest managers who know the land best, removing the barriers that have kept them from doing the work the land demands.”
“Active forest management is not an option. It’s essential,” said Tom Schultz, the forest service chief. “More than 40% of inventoried roadless areas, primarily in the west, have high or very high wildfire hazard potential. And only 5% of those areas have received hazardous fuels reduction treatments since 2014.”
But Craven of the Sierra Club said: “The administration’s attempt to blame the roadless rule for worsening wildfire risk ignores both the facts and the rule itself. Roads generally lead to more ignitions and result in more wildfires – not fewer.
“And, the roadless rule has always allowed for targeted actions to reduce hazardous fuels. What it does not allow is using wildfire as an excuse to open some of America’s most intact public forests to industrial exploitation and new road construction.”
Clinton had championed the roadless rule late in his second term as president after concerns grew around unsustainable logging of national forests.
The biggest roadless area is the Tongass national forest in Alaska, which stores huge amounts of carbon and is home to brown and black bears, wolves and bald eagles.
“America’s last great backcountry forests are not bargaining chips,” Emma Powell, government affairs manager at Alaska Wilderness League, said on Tuesday about the plan. “The Tongass and Chugach national forests are global treasures.
“From fisheries to tourism and outdoor recreation, these landscapes also support thousands of jobs and generate billions in economic activity each year.”
Concerns of environmentalists were especially focussed on logging.
“It’s clear the processes required by the National Environmental Policy Act are being treated as merely boxes to check on the path to enacting an entirely political agenda to clear-cut the last remaining intact old-growth forests in America,” added Maggie Rabb, executive director of the Southeast Alaska Conservation Council.
The public has until 21 September to comment on the plan.
“Trump is pushing for the largest evisceration of public lands protection in American history and against what Americans want,” said Randi Spivak, public lands policy director at the Center for Biological Diversity. “Once you start bulldozing roads for commercial logging and industrial development, there’s no getting them back.”

Bolivia lawmakers likely force economy minister's removal in setback for President Paz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Bolivia lawmakers likely force economy minister's removal in setback for President Paz
LA PAZ, Aug 18 - Bolivia's Congress voted on Tuesday to censure Economy Minister Jose Gabriel Espinoza, a decision President Rodrigo Paz's government said was unconstitutional and signaled would be challenged before the country's top constitutional tribunal.
Presidential spokesperson Jose Luis Galvez said Espinoza could take legal action as soon as Wednesday, suggesting the minister may remain in office while the Constitutional Tribunal reviews the dispute.
Lawmakers backed the motion by majority vote after Espinoza failed to appear before Congress to answer questions on his management of the economy, monetary policy and macroeconomic planning. Espinoza said he had to travel to the city of Santa Cruz to address diesel supply problems before heading to Brazil.
The minister said on Tuesday that he would turn to the nation's top constitutional tribunal to review the decision, arguing that procedures may have been violated.
Under Bolivia's constitution, Paz has 24 hours to remove a censured minister from office. But the government argues the censure vote did not meet constitutional requirements and that the issue should be reviewed by the Constitutional Tribunal before Espinoza is removed.
The dispute raises the stakes in a confrontation between Paz and lawmakers at a delicate moment for his economic reform agenda.
"Tomorrow, the minister in question will take the appropriate actions and may eventually exercise his rights under the Constitution; however, the call is for all procedures to be conducted in accordance with the Constitution," Galvez said.
Galvez said the vote fell short of the constitutional requirement for censure, which he said requires a two-thirds majority, or 111 votes, of the 166-member Congress. Only 91 lawmakers voted to censure Espinoza.
"Any censure resolution issued based on these results is unconstitutional," Galvez said, arguing that internal congressional rules cannot override the constitution.
REFORM AGENDA AT STAKE
The vote comes at a sensitive time for Paz's government, which is seeking congressional backing for economic reforms and for a financing program negotiated with the International Monetary Fund in July that still requires approval from both Bolivia's Congress and the IMF Executive Board.
The program is seen as key to helping stabilize the economy and easing persistent shortages of fuel and foreign currency.
Espinoza said his dismissal reflected "extreme" politicization and cited clashes between the government's work agenda and lawmakers' timelines.
Espinoza has been part of Paz's government since the administration took office in November and has become one of the main architects of the government's economic policy. He has also played a central public role in negotiations with multilateral lenders.
In recent weeks, Espinoza also faced criticism over the alleged purchase of an Audi vehicle at a declared price well below market value. Espinoza said the discrepancy was the result of a paperwork error. REUTERS

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said Tuesday that FIFA had pressed the “self-destruct button” with its failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup.

Swedish MP intervenes in ‘damaging’ Brexit row over elderly Britons ordered to leave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
18:44:06 UTC
03:44:06 KST

The deportation and removal of British citizens from Sweden over Brexit residency rights is damaging relations with the UK amid efforts to improve links with London, a Swedish MP has said.
Håkan Svenneling, representative for Värmland, where a 78-year-old British widow, Joyce Thomas, has been given four weeks to leave Sweden after 21 years of residency, has written to the migration minister, Johan Forssell, asking what he “intends to do to stop the deportations”.
Sevenneling, who is an opposition MP for the left, is to meet Thomas on Wednesday, exactly a week after she was told her appeal had failed over the removal order.
Thomas told the Guardian: “I am in shock. I feel sick. An individual’s life is at stake at my age. It is hell. I have done nothing wrong.”
The retired nurse moved to Sweden with her financier husband, to be closer to one of their sons and their grandchildren, when she was 57.
Her husband, who died of cancer in 2023, did all the administrative work in the household, but both Thomas and her friends have said repeatedly they checked if they had to complete any forms to remain in the country after Brexit, and were told they did not.
Thomas made a late application to remain in Sweden in 2023, just weeks after they returned from the UK, but missing the deadline of 31 December 2021. She and her friends testify that her husband checked whether Brexit was going to affect their residency and they were told they did not need to do anything.
Thomas, who is self sufficient and is not drawing benefit from the Swedish state, has spoken of the “hell” she is now in with the threat of imminent removal, separating her from her family, strong network of friends, and her husband’s grave.
Svenneling says in his letter to Forssell that Britons lawfully in Sweden before the UK’s exit from the EU would see their “existing residency rights continue to apply” under the withdrawal agreement (W/A).
“It was not intended to result in elderly people who had lived in Sweden for decades losing their rights to remain because of a missed deadline or deficiencies in their application [to stay],” he said.
Svenneling’s written parliamentary question adds to growing pressure on the prime minister, Ulf Kristersson’s, centre-right minority coalition to address increasing concerns over the way Sweden is implementing the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, an international, legally binding, treaty.
“The United Kingdom has long been an important partner for Sweden in a wide range of areas. It is clear that the deportations now taking place are damaging bilateral relations between Sweden and the United Kingdom,” Svenneling said.
He raised the case of Thomas, but also of another elderly Briton, Horace (George) Mason, 74, who has dementia and Parkinson’s and is in full-time care. Thomas moved to Sweden 25 years ago to be closer to his son Carl and his grandchildren. He, too, was given four weeks to leave.
His family tried a second legal route for him to remain in Sweden, arguing he had rights, under the European conventionon human rights, to stay close to family on whom he relied. But the migration court of appeal ruled that “the state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs Mason’s interest in continuing to reside” in Sweden.
Writing in the Guardian, David Milstead, who heads the campaign group Brits in Sweden, said the group raised the alarm over Sweden’s approach as far back as 2020 and the safeguards put in place were “untested”.
“Among genuine missed-deadline cases brought to our 9,000-member group, we cannot verify one in which Sweden accepted the reasons for applying late,” he said.
The UK Foreign Office said it has repeatedly raised concerns with the European Commission “that Sweden is taking a considerably stricter approach” to late applications than any other EU member state, with a disproportionate number of refusals.
It said it appeared that “in practice, individuals are not likely to have their reasonable grounds [for a late application] accepted”.
Milstead is concerned that Sweden’s wider migration policy could be affecting decisions made under the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, and has called on the European Commission and Sweden to urgently address the issues.
“Sweden’s migration politics have moved sharply towards restriction. That cannot displace EU law, but it makes remedial action harder to defend politically,” he said.
The migration agency in Sweden said it was unable to discuss individual cases, but that not knowing a Brexit application had to be made to remain in the country was not a “reasonable ground” to stay.
